title: [New Rx] Why Philippine cities should issue their own bonds
summary: Letting credit-worthy Philippine cities issue municipal bonds can fund vital local infrastructure and healthcare, freeing communities from state-bank bottlenecks

blocks.text: On November 13, the Bureau of the Treasury announced a three-year retail dollar bond targeting at least US$200 million, with a minimum investment of US$200. Metrobank pointed to relative calm in oil prices and bond yields as key timing factors. If the national government can ask ordinary savers to lend dollars, similar debt instruments could help local government units (LGUs) finance hospitals, water systems, and infrastructure closer to home.

Asian Development Bank (ADB) president Masato Kanda estimated ASEAN’s infrastructure needs through 2040 at US$7.1 trillion, including US$227 billion for healthcare facilities. Government budgets cover only 45% of these costs. Furthermore, PAGASA’s warning of a strong El Niño persisting into 2027 highlights the need for LGUs to finance water infrastructure. Localities should evaluate leak repairs and water storage projects that can repay loans or municipal bonds through utility fees.

Local bond authority dates back to 1975 for provinces and cities, and the 1991 Local Government Code extended it to municipalities. While cities like Urdaneta and Puerto Princesa have issued bonds, state-bank borrowing still dominates. For instance, Urdaneta pursued a ₱500 million LandBank loan in 2026 rather than issuing new bonds.

ADB studies show state banks offer rates close to the national government’s borrowing cost. Because bonds involve legal, underwriting, and disclosure expenses, they must offer distinct advantages — such as longer fixed-rate terms or broader investor reach. The World Bank notes that weak project preparation remains a primary bottleneck for LGU borrowing. Regional peers offer useful models: Vietnam has piloted municipal green bonds for water projects, while Jakarta has prepared revenue bond offerings.

Approved Official Development Assistance (ODA) projects often stall due to missing or delayed national budget counterpart funds. DEPDev’s 2024 portfolio review highlighted a ₱13.98 billion gap between counterpart needs and available allocations. Where agreements assign a share to creditworthy LGUs, municipal revenue bonds could fund those local contributions for income-generating utilities, as permitted under Section 299 of the Local Government Code.

To succeed, local issuance should start with credit-worthy LGUs and revenue-generating projects like water systems or public markets. Requirements must include audited accounts, independent credit ratings, and robust debt-service coverage. Investors could range from domestic commercial banks and institutional funds to retail savers.

Prior to issuance, LGUs must secure land titles, complete engineering designs, and enforce strict procurement rules. Cities maintain financial discipline through national oversight and the statutory 20%-of-regular-income debt-service limit.

Zero-coupon bonds secured by sinking funds or patrimonial land offer another viable structure, as demonstrated by Victorias, Negros Occidental, which successfully issued and repaid housing bonds. Looking ahead, Congress could authorize broader general obligation bonds for creditworthy LGUs to finance essential non-revenue infrastructure like flood control.

Two options exist for financing healthcare expansion. First, Congress could authorize PhilHealth to issue short-term general obligation bonds backed by general revenues to manage emergency cash-flow needs or launch new health benefits. Second, public specialty hospital corporations could issue revenue bonds backed by receipts from premium private amenities.

Following models from Singapore’s National University Hospital and Bangkok’s Siriraj Piyamaharajkarun Hospital, surplus proceeds from paying patients could cross-subsidize public wards while preserving the Universal Health Care Act’s mandated basic bed quotas (90% in government hospitals and 70% in specialty centers).

The treasury knows how to reach savers. Let credit-worthy LGUs do the same for projects ready to build and able to repay. Their delivery record should determine how far the market grows. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is a physician, healthcare investor, and adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines Manila College of Public Health. His New Rx column examines Philippine healthcare and public policy through a Korean and regional Asian lens.
